title: Joshua 7:16–26
context: Joshua 7:16–26 carries out the procedure of 7:14–15. The sacred selection moves from Judah to the Zerahites, to Zabdi’s household, and finally to Achan. Joshua calls on him to give glory to the LORD by confessing, and Achan admits that he saw, coveted, took and hid the plunder. The goods are recovered and laid before the LORD, and Achan, his household and possessions are brought to the valley of Achor, where the sentence is carried out and a heap of stones is raised. The LORD turns from his anger. The name Achor plays on the Hebrew word for “trouble” (7:25), and the place later becomes a symbol of hope restored (Hosea 2:15). The passage is grim, and it is best read within its covenant setting at the start of Israel’s life in the land.

verses.text: So Joshua rose up early in the morning and brought Israel near by their tribes. The tribe of Judah was selected.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua rises “early in the morning,” as he did before Jericho (6:12), and carries out the LORD’s instructions without delay. Judah, the leading tribe, is selected first. Arminian readers note Joshua’s prompt obedience, the response the situation required, and observe that the process narrows step by step, giving every opportunity for honesty before the end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the selection of Judah, the royal tribe, as a reminder that no tribe or status exempts anyone from God’s searching judgment. God’s holiness applies without favoritism. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing Joshua’s obedience and as the first step in God’s exposure of hidden sin, a process both see as just and orderly rather than arbitrary.

verses.text: He brought near the family of Judah, and he selected the family of the Zerahites. He brought near the family of the Zerahites man by man, and Zabdi was selected.
verses.arminianNotes: The selection moves from the tribe of Judah to the family of the Zerahites and then to Zabdi. Arminian readers note how the narrowing creates suspense and keeps Achan before the reader as the one who knows but stays silent. His silence through each stage underscores his responsibility and the hardening effect of concealed sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s precise knowledge at work, moving with certainty toward the one who sinned. No one escapes his gaze, however large the crowd. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the LORD sees through the community to the individual, and that corporate responsibility in 7:1 does not erase personal guilt.

verses.text: He brought near his household man by man, and Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was selected.
verses.arminianNotes: Achan is finally identified, with the full genealogy repeated from 7:1: “the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah.” Arminian readers note that the repetition closes the circle the narrator opened, and that God brought the matter to light even though Achan had not come forward on his own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as underscoring that God’s judgment is accurate and individual: he knows Achan by name and lineage. The chronicler later remembers him as “Achar, the troubler of Israel” (1 Chronicles 2:7). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the fulfillment of 7:14 and as a solemn reminder that each person stands accountable before God.

verses.text: Joshua said to Achan, “My son, please give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make confession to him. Tell me now what you have done! Don’t hide it from me!”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua addresses Achan gently, “My son,” and urges him to “give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make confession to him.” Arminian readers note the pastoral tone even in judgment, and the call to a real response. Confession here honors God by agreeing with his verdict, and the wisdom of Proverbs 28:13 applies: “whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that “give glory to the LORD” functions as a solemn charge to tell the truth before God (compare John 9:24, “Give glory to God”). Confession acknowledges that God’s judgment is right. Shared ground: both traditions see confession as honoring God, and both note that the text does not tell us what Achan’s confession meant for his standing before God beyond this life, so readers should not overstate either way.

verses.text: Achan answered Joshua, and said, “I have truly sinned against the LORD, the God of Israel, and this is what I have done.
verses.arminianNotes: Achan answers, “I have truly sinned against the LORD, the God of Israel.” Arminian readers note that the confession is direct and names the offense as against God first. It is a genuine admission, though it comes only after he has been identified, which shows how concealment can delay repentance until exposure forces the issue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the God-ward focus of the confession, consistent with Scripture’s teaching that sin is primarily against God. The admission vindicates the LORD’s verdict in 7:11. Shared ground: both traditions read the confession as truthful and as part of what restores Israel’s relationship with God, while noting that the text leaves Achan’s inner state to God.

verses.text: When I saw among the plunder a beautiful Babylonian robe, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold weighing fifty shekels, then I coveted them and took them. Behold, they are hidden in the ground in the middle of my tent, with the silver under it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Achan traces his sin in sequence: “I saw,” “I coveted,” “took,” and hid. The pattern recalls the progression of temptation elsewhere in Scripture. In Hebrew the robe is literally a robe of Shinar, which the WEB renders “Babylonian.” A WEB footnote notes that a shekel is about 10 grams (about 0.35 ounces), so the silver weighed about 2 kilograms and the gold about half a kilogram. Arminian readers stress the stages at which Achan could have turned back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the sequence the way sin moves from the eye to the heart to the hand, with covetousness at the root, as the tenth commandment warns and as Deuteronomy 7:25 warned about plunder: “You shall not covet the silver or the gold.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a classic portrait of temptation and as a warning that hidden sin is not truly hidden from God.

verses.text: So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent. Behold, it was hidden in his tent, with the silver under it.
verses.arminianNotes: Messengers run to the tent and find everything as Achan said: “it was hidden in his tent, with the silver under it.” Arminian readers note that the haste of the messengers reflects the urgency of removing the devoted thing so that Israel can be restored. The confirmation shows Achan’s confession was truthful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the discovery publicly confirms God’s verdict and Achan’s confession. Nothing was left to rumor or suspicion; the evidence was found where the guilty man said it was. Shared ground: both traditions see due process in the narrative, as identification, confession and confirming evidence all come together before the sentence is carried out.

verses.text: They took them from the middle of the tent, and brought them to Joshua and to all the children of Israel. They laid them down before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The goods are brought to Joshua and all Israel and laid “down before the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the stolen things are returned to the one to whom they belonged, since they had been devoted to the LORD. The whole community witnesses the act, which helps restore its integrity and trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the placing of the goods before the LORD as an acknowledgment of his rightful claim: what was devoted to him is restored to his presence. The act is liturgical as well as judicial. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the public reversal of Achan’s secret theft and as a step toward the restoration of God’s favor.

verses.text: Joshua, and all Israel with him, took Achan the son of Zerah, the silver, the robe, the wedge of gold, his sons, his daughters, his cattle, his donkeys, his sheep, his tent, and all that he had; and they brought them up to the valley of Achor.
verses.arminianNotes: Achan is brought to the valley of Achor with the goods, “his sons, his daughters,” livestock, tent, “and all that he had.” Arminian readers acknowledge the difficulty this verse raises. The law elsewhere forbids putting children to death for a parent’s sin (Deuteronomy 24:16), and interpreters differ on whether the family shared in the deed, perhaps through the concealment in the tent, or on how far the following verse includes them in the sentence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the difficulty seriously, noting that the text presents this as a unique judgment involving devoted things at the start of the conquest, where the offender became “devoted” himself (7:12, 15). Shared ground: both traditions refuse to soften the narrative or to make it a general rule, and both read it in light of Deuteronomy 24:16 and Ezekiel 18:20, which affirm individual responsibility in ordinary justice.

verses.text: Joshua said, “Why have you troubled us? The LORD will trouble you today.” All Israel stoned him with stones, and they burned them with fire and stoned them with stones.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua’s words, “Why have you troubled us? The LORD will trouble you today,” play on the name Achor (trouble) and recall the warning that taking devoted things would “trouble” the camp (6:18). Arminian readers see the sentence as the just consequence of a freely chosen act, executed by the whole community, which owned its responsibility for purging the sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the whole of Israel carries out the sentence, signaling that the community must deal with sin in its midst. The pronouns shift from “him” to “them,” part of what leaves interpreters uncertain about the scope of the sentence. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sobering judgment in Israel’s theocratic setting, not a model for the church, which is told, “Purge out the old yeast,” through discipline (1 Corinthians 5:7).

verses.text: They raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. The LORD turned from the fierceness of his anger. Therefore the name of that place was called “The valley of Achor” to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: A heap of stones marks the place, and “The LORD turned from the fierceness of his anger,” language that echoes Deuteronomy 13:17. Arminian readers note that God’s anger is real but not endless; when sin is dealt with, he turns in mercy. The valley of Achor later becomes “a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15), showing that God can transform a place of judgment into a place of renewal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that God’s wrath was turned aside only when the sin was dealt with, a pattern that points ahead to the cross, where Christ bore the curse for his people (Galatians 3:13). Shared ground: both traditions read the memorial as a lasting warning, both welcome Hosea’s promise of hope from Achor, and both see the chapter’s end as the restoration that makes chapter 8 possible.
